name: Wilawila
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: Carr, Therese L. 2000. Wunambal: a language of the North-West Kimberley region, Western Australia. MA (Hons) thesis, University of New England. (Section 2.4 Stress, pp.61ff.)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Nearest described Northern Worrorran relative (Wunambal, wuna1249), not Wilawila: 'In words of more than 3 syllables primary stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable, and secondary stress on the first syllable.. Two syllable words are stressed in the first syllable.. Three syllable words are normally stressed on the first syllable'. Mentions Wilawila speakers absorbed into the Wunambal community and D. Utemorrah's 1989-90 KLRC Wilawila notes (tapes destroyed) but gives no Wilawila stress data.

sources.citation: Capell, A. & H.H.J. Coate. 1984. Comparative studies in Northern Kimberley languages. Pacific Linguistics C-69. Canberra: Research School of Pacific Studies, ANU. xv+262+21 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: The only description containing Wilawila data. Ch.1 'Preliminary: phonological principles' (pp.7-19: phonemic systems, root/word, syllable, morphophonemic rules) has NO stress/accent section and no placement rule for any NK language. Only incidental remarks: Intro p.4 (discussion of Ngarinjin dialects, which there includes 'a dialect of the northern group known as Wilawila or Walmbi'): 'ma ra angul ro:n (with advanced accent), one of the very rare accents on a final syllable'; p.83-84 (Worora nouns): 'The fixity of the stress is noticeable also, even if it has to fall four syllables back from…

sources.citation: HathiTrust record 000621077 (Capell & Coate 1984; htids mdp.39015013265460, uva.x001066922; Full view, CC-BY-NC-ND) and HTRC Extracted Features page-token files for both copies
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Used only to locate the pages of C-69 containing 'stress'/'accent' tokens (seq 24, 33, 271-273 etc.) before the PDF was obtained; HathiTrust page viewer itself blocks automated access.

sources.citation: McGregor, William B. & Alan Rumsey. 2009. Worrorran revisited: the case for genetic relations among languages of the Northern Kimberley region of Western Australia. Pacific Linguistics 600. Canberra: ANU.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Wilawila listed as 'no surviving speakers', sources = 'Capell and Coate (1984)' only, 'poorly attested Wilawila (which appears to show some characteristics of Eastern and some of Northern Worrorran)'. Comparative phonology chapter mentions 'initial stressed syllables' only in passing (Unggumi vowels); no stress statement for Wilawila or the family.

sources.citation: McGregor, William B. 1988. Handbook of Kimberley languages, Vol. 1: General information. Pacific Linguistics C-105. Canberra: ANU. Section 5.16 Wilawila.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Inventory of materials only: 'People who have worked intensively on the language: No one'; 'Grammar or sketch grammar: None; Capell & Coate (1984) contains some information'; word list SIL 1971 (AIAS tapes A2185, 2186; pMs 1759); Glasgow, Hocking & Steiner n.d. survey report. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Capell, A. 1941. Notes on the Wunambal language. Oceania 11(3): 295-308.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No mention of stress or accent; no Wilawila material.

sources.citation: Capell, A. 1940. The classification of languages in north and north-west Australia. Oceania 10(3): 241-272 (contd. 10(4)).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: General areal remark only, p.243: 'Accent is also important, though it is difficult to set down rules for it.' p.259 treats Wilawila as an Ungarinyin dialect 'spoken in the country known as Barurungari or Walmbi, along the upper Drysdale'. No stress rule.

sources.citation: McGregor, William B. 2004. The Languages of the Kimberley, Western Australia. London & New York: RoutledgeCurzon. xxvi+371 pp. (phonology chapter)
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: a digital copy exists, paywalled at the publisher; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL7091.K55 M36 2004)
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL7091.K55 M36 2004
sources.note: Areal overview by the leading Kimberley specialist; its phonology chapter gives a general statement on word stress in Kimberley/Worrorran languages that would be the best available family-level (second-hand) proxy for undescribed Wilawila.

sources.citation: Utemorrah, Daisy. 1989-1990. Unpublished KLRC notes on Wilawila (with Geoffrey Manglamara), Kimberley Language Resource Centre, Halls Creek (per Carr 2000:11, most tapes destroyed).
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Only other first-hand Wilawila documentation reported; surviving notes might include stress-marked forms.
